a2.full_story_text:
Here is the strange part of laundry: a towel can come out of the washer, dry, and still smell like damp cloth.

This pattern appeared in a 2022 survey of 359 households. People reported laundry smells at different stages: 110 households reported a smell before washing, 91 while the laundry was still wet after washing, and 73 after drying. These groups could overlap.

A separate study followed new cotton towels in 26 Japanese households for six months. Smell and a dull look appeared after two months. Researchers also found a growing sticky layer inside the towel threads, especially in the lengthwise threads.

So the mystery is not only what the washing machine removes. It is also what may stay hidden inside the fabric.
a2.point_one_text:
When the fabric changes the route
Cotton and polyester do not behave in the same way. In a lab model, polyester held more skin oil and more bacteria tightly. Cotton held more water, and some bacteria stayed active after drying. In both fabrics, bacteria inside the threads could build a sticky layer that was hard to wash away. So no single fabric alone predicts odor: cotton may keep moisture, while polyester may hold more oil and bacteria.
a2.point_two_text:
A wash is not a simple switch
A wash is not just clean or dirty. At 30 or 40 degrees without bleach, some bacteria survived and moved between fabrics. Active-oxygen bleach reduced more microbes in 30 minutes. At 60 degrees, all tested microbes were reduced. In five home washing machines, nearly all bacterial groups found before washing remained on cotton after a 30-degree cycle without bleach. The same mild process may therefore leave the same problem.

b1b.full_story_text:
A towel can come out of the wash looking clean, then give off a wet-cloth or old-rag smell. That smell may be noticed before washing, while the fabric is still wet after washing, or after the laundry has dried, and these stages can overlap.

A 2022 survey asked 359 households about laundry odors. About 110 reported a smell before washing, while fewer noticed one in wet laundry after washing or after the laundry had dried. These groups could overlap, so the numbers are not a rate for all households. But they show that the wash cycle does not always mark the end of the story.

Why can the smell return? In laboratory models using cotton and polyester, bacteria linked with skin oil and sweat could move into the fibers and build a sticky layer called a biofilm. That layer was difficult to remove with ordinary washing, and odor could remain after the wash.

In another cotton-cloth model, a particular combination of three bacteria produced a stronger and longer-lasting wet-cloth smell than single bacteria or other combinations.

A separate six-month study followed new cotton towels in 26 Japanese households. Smell and dullness were already observed after two months. During the study, biofilm structures were seen mainly around the towels’ lengthwise threads. The layer’s components and the number of bacteria that could be grown in the lab also increased over time.

This was what researchers observed in those homes. It does not mean that every towel will smell after two months.
b1b.point_one_text:
When fabric and drying join forces
There is another twist: drying and fabric type work together. In lab tests, prolonged or slow drying was linked with stronger odor, while high-humidity drying was associated with characteristic laundry odor. Polyester held more skin oil and more strongly attached bacteria, while cotton held more water; some bacterial activity continued after drying. Softener-treated cotton also absorbed less water. So the same detergent routine can end differently on different fabrics.
b1b.point_two_text:
The washing machine joins the story
Washing is an exchange, not a reset. In tests, bacteria survived and moved between fabrics during bleach-free washing; bleach-containing conditions reduced them more. In five household machines, bacteria moved among water, clothes, and machine surfaces, while prewash groups remained on washed cotton. Machine parts also carried many bacteria. Another comparison found no clear link between total bacterial makeup and machine odor. The towel may be one part of the system.

a2.full_story_text:
A small slider inside the refrigerator may be easy to ignore.

But many crisper drawers have two settings: low humidity and high humidity. They are not simply two names for the same space.

The low setting lets more air move through the drawer. The high setting is more closed.

That small difference can matter after fresh food comes home from the store.

Some foods give off a gas as they ripen. Other foods lose water quickly and become soft or limp. The two drawer settings are meant for these different problems.

There is also one important surprise. The best choice is not always as simple as “fruit goes here” and “vegetables go there.”

And before choosing a setting, there is another question: does this food belong in the refrigerator at all?
a2.point_one_text:
Ask what the food is trying to lose
A useful way to use the slider is to ask one question: “Am I trying to keep water in, or let a gas out?”

If the main problem is wilting, high humidity is the better match. Leafy greens, such as kale, and broccoli can lose water quickly, so a more closed drawer can help.

If the main problem is gas, low humidity may be the better match. Apples and pears give off ethylene, a gas that can make nearby produce ripen too quickly. More air movement helps that gas escape.

This turns the slider into a simple diagnosis tool. You do not have to memorize a fruit-and-vegetable rule. You can look at the food’s main storage problem.
a2.point_two_text:
The drawer is not always the first step
Humidity settings cannot help food that is not suited to refrigerator storage.

Tomatoes and bananas are recommended for counter storage, not for a low-humidity drawer. Potatoes, sweet potatoes, onions, and garlic do not need refrigeration and are better kept in a cool, dry place.

So even the low-humidity advice for apples and pears should not be copied to every food that gives off ethylene. First choose the right storage place. Then choose the setting.

b1b.full_story_text:
At first glance, a crisper drawer looks like a simple box for fresh food. But many refrigerators have two settings: low humidity and high humidity. Some models use a slider to adjust them.

That small choice changes the air inside the drawer. The low-humidity setting allows more air to move through. The high-humidity setting is closer to sealed.

Used well, these settings can help fresh produce keep its quality longer. But the right choice is not simply “fruit here, vegetables there.”

Fresh food can lose quality in different ways. Some foods release a gas as they ripen. That gas can make nearby produce ripen too quickly. Other foods lose water quickly and begin to wilt.

So the useful question is not only, “Is this a fruit or a vegetable?”

It is also, “What problem am I trying to prevent?”
b1b.point_one_text:
Sort by the risk, not by the food group
A practical way to choose the setting is to look at the food’s main risk.

Apples and pears are good low-humidity examples. They release more ripening gas, and extra airflow can help move it away.

Leafy greens, such as kale, and vegetables that lose water easily, such as broccoli, fit the high-humidity side better. Keeping more moisture around them can help slow wilting.

This gives you a simple rule for foods you may not know well: think about whether you are trying to limit early ripening or prevent moisture loss. That is more useful than memorizing a long list of fruits and vegetables.
b1b.point_two_text:
The drawer is not the first decision
There is one important boundary. Choosing low or high humidity only matters after you decide that the food belongs in the refrigerator.

Tomatoes and bananas are recommended for counter storage rather than refrigeration. So they should not go in the low-humidity drawer simply because they release ripening gas.

Potatoes, sweet potatoes, onions, and garlic do not need refrigeration. They are recommended for a cool, dry environment. That is not exactly the same as keeping them on the counter with tomatoes and bananas.

The larger lesson is simple: first choose the right storage place, then choose the right drawer setting.
